step: -3-2-10123456Sketch, not to scale Find the integer values of x satisfying x^2 - 3x - 10 < 0. How many are there?
why: The sketch's number-line tick labels are flattened into a meaningless run-on string ('-3-2-10123456') jammed straight against 'Sketch, not to scale' and the question. A struggling student reads it as a garbled number and has to re-read to find where the actual question begins.
fix: Strip the flattened axis digits from the question text so it reads cleanly, e.g. '(Sketch, not to scale.) Find the integer values of x satisfying x^2 - 3x - 10 < 0. How many are there?'

step: 0123456Sketch, not to scale Solve x^2 - 6x + 5 < 0. How many integer values of x satisfy this?
why: Same problem: the number-line tick labels ('0123456') are run together and jammed against 'Sketch, not to scale' and the question, forcing a re-read to locate the start of the actual task.
fix: Remove the flattened axis digits so it reads cleanly, e.g. '(Sketch, not to scale.) Solve x^2 - 6x + 5 < 0. How many integer values of x satisfy this?'

step: Substitute y = 3 and clear the fraction: 3 × (x − 1). Work out 3 × 1 = [box=3]
why: The instruction crams three actions (substitute, clear the fraction, show 3 × (x − 1)) and then abruptly asks for 3 × 1, whose link to the shown expression (x − 1, not 1) is never explained. A struggling student cannot see why they are multiplying 3 by 1, so the trivial box (=3) becomes confusing rather than guiding.
fix: Split and connect it: e.g. 'Multiply out 3(x − 1). The number part is 3 × 1 = [3], so 3(x − 1) = 3x − 3.'

step: Substitute y = 3 and clear the fraction: 3 × (x + 1). Work out 3 × 1 = [box=3]
why: Same overloaded phrasing as gold[0]: the jump from '3 × (x + 1)' to the asked '3 × 1' has no bridge, so the student has to re-read to work out what the box is even for and why the (x + 1) became 1.
fix: Reword to make the expansion explicit: 'Multiply out 3(x + 1). The number part is 3 × 1 = [3], so 3(x + 1) = 3x + 3.'

step: What is left: 150 − 120 = 30, and 30 ÷ 6 = [box=5]
why: The step opens with a fragment ('What is left:') and chains a completed statement (150 − 120 = 30) with the actually-asked computation using 'and', so a weaker student may hesitate over whether the box wants 30 or the answer to 30 ÷ 6.
fix: Separate the two: 'Now find what is left: 150 − 120 = 30. Then 30 ÷ 6 = [5].'

step: so (x+3)² = 7, and comparing with −3 + √k gives k =
why: The walk gets to (x+3)² = 7 and then jumps straight to the surd form −3 + √k to read off k. Taking the square root of both sides and rearranging to x = −3 + √7 is never shown, so a struggling student has no way to see WHY k = 7 — it looks like the answer appears from nowhere.
fix: Insert an intermediate step, e.g. 'square-root both sides: x + 3 = √7, so x = −3 + √7; matching −3 + √k gives k =' before the final box.

step: 4ac = 4·k·k = 4k². Set 36 − 4k² = 0, so 4k² =
why: One box carries three separate moves (write 4ac symbolically, form the equation 36 − 4k² = 0, then rearrange) and it switches to '·' for multiply when every other problem in the pack uses '×'. A weaker student may not read '·' as multiplication and will have to re-read the whole line to find what the box actually wants.
fix: Split into two steps and use ×: 'work out 4ac: 4 × k × k = 4k²' then 'set 36 − 4k² = 0 and rearrange, so 4k² ='.

step: positive root: (-3 + 6.08) ÷ 2 =
why: The final answer is a decimal but the box is 'NO label', whereas the identical final-root step in silver[2] and gold[3] carries label:'(a decimal)'. The inconsistency means a student here gets no signal that the answer is not a whole number and may wrongly round.
fix: add label '(a decimal)'

step: larger root: (5 + 4.12) ÷ 4 =
why: Same as silver[0]: the final decimal root box has no '(a decimal)' hint even though the matching step in silver[2] and gold[3] does, so the expected form (a decimal, not a whole number) is left unsignalled.
fix: add label '(a decimal)'

step: the constant added on is minus that square: 0 − 9 =
why: 'the constant added on is minus that square' is a convoluted back-reference. A struggling student has to unpick which 'square' and why it becomes negative before they can even attempt the '0 − 9' arithmetic.
fix: Reword plainly, e.g. 'you subtract that square from 0: 0 − 9 ='.

step: Total quarters: 28 + 2 + 1 =  [box=31]
why: The three boxes the student has just filled are 16, 8 and 4 (the whole terms in quarters). The final sum then reads '28 + 2 + 1' — but none of those three numbers matches the boxes just computed. 28 is an unnamed running subtotal (16+8+4) that was never shown as a step, and the 2 and 1 are the 1/2 and 1/4 terms converted into quarters — a conversion the walk never builds (the intro only lists the raw fractions 1/2, 1/4). A struggling student who has typed 16, 8, 4 will stare at '28 + 2 + 1' with no idea where any of the three numbers came from.
fix: Add explicit conversion asks for the fractional terms and name the subtotal, e.g. 'Half in quarters: 1/2 = [box=2]', 'Quarter in quarters: 1/4 = [box=1]', then 'Add the whole parts: 16 + 8 + 4 = [box=28]', then 'Total quarters: 28 + 2 + 1 = [box=31]'.

step: First gap is 8 - k; second gap is (2k + 1) - 8 = 2k - 7. Set 8 - k = 2k - 7, add k to both sides: 8 = 3k - 7. Add 7: 3k =  [box=15]
why: This single ask stacks four separate algebra moves before the one box the student must fill: form the second gap and simplify it, set the two gaps equal, add k to both sides, then add 7. A struggling 15-year-old has to re-read the whole line to locate what '3k = ' actually depends on, and any slip in the reasoning above is invisible because there is no box to check it against.
fix: Break it into staged asks with their own boxes: 'Second gap: (2k + 1) - 8 = 2k - [box=7]', then 'Set the gaps equal: 8 - k = 2k - 7. Add k to both sides: 8 = 3k - [box=7]', then 'Add 7 to both sides: 3k = [box=15]'.

step: Split the middle: 2x² + 6x − x − 3, group to 2x(x+3) − 1(x+3) = (2x − 1)(x + 3). Set 2x − 1 = 0: 2x = 1, x = [box=0.5, NO label]
why: The prose ends '2x = 1, x =', which naturally leads a struggling student to write the fraction 1/2 rather than the expected decimal 0.5. With no label the correct-value answer gets marked wrong on format alone.
fix: Add label '(a decimal)' to the box.

step: group to 5x(x−2) + 1(x−2) = (5x + 1)(x − 2). Set 5x + 1 = 0: 5x = −1, x = [box=-0.2, NO label]
why: '5x = −1, x =' invites the answer −1/5; a struggling student is unlikely to convert to −0.2 unprompted, so a right value fails on format.
fix: Add label '(a decimal)' to the box.

step: group to 5x(x+1) − 2(x+1) = (5x − 2)(x + 1). Set 5x − 2 = 0: 5x = 2, x = [box=0.4, NO label]
why: '5x = 2, x =' points a student at 2/5, not the expected decimal 0.4; no label to signal the required form.
fix: Add label '(a decimal)' to the box.

why: '4x = −1, x =' leads to −1/4; without a label the student won't know the box wants −0.25 rather than the fraction.
fix: Add label '(a decimal)' to the box.

step: Set the first bracket to 0: 2x + 1 = 0, 2x = −1, x = [box=-0.5, NO label]  /  Set the second bracket to 0: 2x − 1 = 0, 2x = 1, x = [box=0.5, NO label]
why: Both boxes follow '2x = −1' / '2x = 1', which cue the fractions −1/2 and 1/2; neither box tells the student the answer must be a decimal (−0.5 / 0.5).
fix: Add label '(a decimal)' to both boxes.

step: Split the middle: 2x² + 6x − x − 3, group to 2x(x+3) − 1(x+3) = (2x − 1)(x + 3). Set 2x − 1 = 0: 2x = 1, x = [box=0.5]
why: This single step crams five operations (rewrite middle term, group, factor each group, combine brackets, then solve one bracket) into one sentence the student must re-read before they can find what the box actually wants. Recurs identically across gold[0]–gold[3].
fix: Split into two steps: one that ends at '= (2x − 1)(x + 3) = 0', then a separate step 'Set 2x − 1 = 0: 2x = 1, x = ___'.

step: So 3(x² − 4) = 0. Divide by 3: x² − 4 = 0, a difference of two squares (x+2)(x−2) = 0. Set x + 2 = 0: x = [box=-2]
why: One step bundles dividing by 3, recognising the difference of two squares, factorising, and solving a bracket — too much to hold before answering.
fix: Break into two steps: '3(x² − 4) = 0, divide by 3 → x² − 4 = 0 = (x+2)(x−2) = 0', then 'Set x + 2 = 0: x = ___'.

step: Multiply a by c: 2 × (−3) = −6. Find two numbers that multiply to −6 and add to +5: 6 and [box=-1, NO label]
why: 'a' and 'c' refer to the coefficients of ax²+bx+c, but the walk never establishes that a/b/c naming (the intro says 'multiply the ends'). A struggling student meets undefined labels. The concrete '2 × (−3)' partly rescues it, hence low. Recurs across all four gold problems.
fix: Replace 'Multiply a by c' with 'Multiply the two ends (the number in front of x² and the last number): 2 × (−3) = −6'.

step: Middle term of (x+4)²: 2 × 4 =  [box=8, label:'x']
why: Every earlier walk (silver[0], gold[0]) builds the middle term by working out the Outer and Inner products SEPARATELY and adding them (e.g. 3x + 4x). This squared-bracket walk instead jumps straight to the '2 ×' doubling shortcut for a perfect square without ever explaining it. A struggling student who has only been shown FOIL will not know why the middle term is 2 × 4 rather than 4 + 4, so the reasoning is presupposed rather than built.
fix: Add an intro line before the ask, e.g. 'In (x+4)² the two middle products are both x × 4 = 4x, and 4x + 4x = 2 × 4 = 8x.' Then keep the 2 × 4 ask. (Same shortcut recurs for (x+2)² just below.)

step: and 1 + 7 + 12 =  [box=20, NO label]
why: The intro only sets up ONE substitution: 'Check by putting x = 1 into the original brackets', which the previous step does (5 × 4 = 20). This step then checks the OTHER side — x = 1 into the expansion x² + 7x + 12 — but that is never framed. A struggling student sees a bare 'and 1 + 7 + 12 =' and may not realise where the 1, 7 and 12 come from. The same unframed back-reference appears in gold[0] as 'and 6 + 11 − 10 ='.
fix: Add a short intro before this ask, e.g. 'Now put x = 1 into your expansion x² + 7x + 12: that is 1 + 7 + 12.' Then both sides should match at 20.

step: Replace y: 2x + (3x - 1). Collect the x terms: 2x + 3x =  [box=5, label:'x']
why: This single ask stacks two separate instructions (substitute y, then collect like terms) plus a compressed expression '2x + (3x - 1)' onto one line. Every other step in the pack is one short instruction; this is the densest and forces a struggling student to re-read to work out what to actually do. It is also the pack's only substitution problem, so the method is unfamiliar, making the packed wording harder to parse.
fix: Split into two steps: (1) 'Replace y with (3x - 1). The equation becomes 2x + (3x - 1) = 14.' then (2) 'Collect the x terms: 2x + 3x = [box, label:x]'.

step: Move the 6 across and tidy so x² is positive; the constant term becomes [box=6, NO label]
why: The intro line immediately above this ask already displays 'So x² - 5x + 6 = 0', so the answer (+6) is on screen before the student is asked to produce it — a struggling student will be confused about what is being asked. The step also bundles two sign operations (move the 6 across from 5x - x² = 6, then negate to make x² positive) into one clause.
fix: Reorder so this ask comes BEFORE the 'So x² - 5x + 6 = 0' reveal, or reword to derive from the earlier line: 'Starting from 5x - x² = 6, move every term to the left and make x² positive; the constant term becomes ▢.'

step: Two single fractions equal each other, so cross multiply: multiply the left top by 2 and the right top by 3.
why: This is the first appearance of cross-multiplication, and the walk tells the student to multiply by 2 and 3 without ever saying those numbers are the OTHER fraction's denominators. A struggling student cannot see where 2 and 3 come from or generalise the method. The same unexplained move recurs in gold[2] and gold[4].
fix: Add one building sentence at first use: 'Cross multiply means each top is multiplied by the other fraction's bottom: (5x + 2) times the right bottom 2, and (3x + 8) times the left bottom 3.'

step: Cross multiply: the left top times 2, the right top times 5. Left: 2 × 2(x − 1) = 4(x − 1). Expand the left: 4 × (−1) =
why: The ask is very long and buries the actual question (4 × (−1)) at the end after stated working. The notation '2 × 2(x − 1)' uses two different 2s (the cross-multiply factor and the coefficient inside the bracket), which is easy to misread; the student then has to spot that the 4 they multiply came from '2 × 2'.
fix: Split it up. Say separately: 'The left top is 2(x − 1); multiply it by 2 to get 4(x − 1).' Then ask on its own short line: 'Expand: 4 × (−1) ='.

step: Expand both brackets. First 5(2x + 1) = 10x + 5. Now the tricky one: −3 × (−2) =
why: The ask states one bracket's full expansion as a given fact and then buries the real question (−3 × (−2)) at the very end. A struggling student has to read past working they are not being asked to do, then isolate the single negative-times-negative they must answer.
fix: Give the first bracket in an intro, then make the ask just the question: 'Expand −3(x − 2). The tricky part is a negative times a negative: −3 × (−2) ='.

step: Expand both sides. Left: 3(2x + 1) = 6x + 3. Right: 2 × (4x − 3) then + 3. 2 × (−3) =
why: 'Right: 2 × (4x − 3) then + 3' is awkward and hard to parse, and the arithmetic the student actually answers (2 × (−3)) sits at the end of a long line of stated working, so the question is easy to lose.
fix: Reword and separate: 'Expand 2(4x − 3) to get 8x − 6, then add the +3 that follows.' Then ask on its own line: '2 × (−3) ='.

step: Now 4(x + 1) + 3(x − 1) = 36. Expand: 4x + 4 + 3x − 3 = 36. Combine: 7x + 1 = 36. Subtract 1 from both sides.
why: This single intro silently expands two brackets AND combines like terms in one dense line with no intermediate box to answer. A struggling student has a lot to follow before the next ask.
fix: Break into two beats: first show the expansion (4x + 4 + 3x − 3 = 36), then a separate line to combine into 7x + 1 = 36 before subtracting 1.

step: The whole left side is divided by 5. Multiply both sides by 5 to clear it. 5 × 5 =
why: The ask repeats the whole intro sentence verbatim before the arithmetic, making a long prompt the student re-reads for no new information. The same repeat-the-intro pattern appears in silver[3] and silver[6].
fix: Since the intro already explained it, keep the ask to the arithmetic: 'Multiply both sides by 5: 5 × 5 ='.

step: The x term is negative, so add 3x to both sides. That gives 20 = 5 + 3x. Now subtract 5 from both sides: 20 − 5 =
why: This one ask bundles two algebra moves (add 3x, then subtract 5) and quietly flips x to the right-hand side (20 = 5 + 3x) before the student answers a plain 20 − 5. Two conceptual steps compressed into a box worth one subtraction is a lot to hold.
fix: Split into two beats: an intro/ask that lands '20 = 5 + 3x' from adding 3x, then a separate ask 'Subtract 5: 20 − 5 ='.

step: (2, 3)(5, 4)(2, −3)(5, −4) Describe the single transformation that maps (2, 3) to (2, −3) and (5, 4) to (5, −4).
why: The stem opens with four coordinate pairs run together with no spaces, labels or punctuation ('(2, 3)(5, 4)(2, −3)(5, −4)') before the sentence begins. A struggling reader meets this as unexplained clutter and cannot tell it apart from the actual instruction, so re-reads to find where the question really starts.
fix: Delete the leading coordinate string (it looks like leaked diagram/plot data); the sentence 'Describe the single transformation that maps (2, 3) to (2, −3) and (5, 4) to (5, −4).' already contains every coordinate needed.

step: (1, 4)(4, −1) Describe the single transformation mapping (1, 4) to (4, −1).
why: The stem starts with '(1, 4)(4, −1)' jammed together before the sentence, duplicating the coordinates that appear again inside the instruction. The reader has to skip an unlabelled coordinate fragment to reach the readable question.
fix: Remove the leading '(1, 4)(4, −1)'; the sentence 'Describe the single transformation mapping (1, 4) to (4, −1).' is self-contained.

step: centre (2, 1)G (5, 3) Point G(5, 3) is enlarged by scale factor −1, centre (2, 1). What are the coordinates of G'?
why: The stem opens with 'centre (2, 1)G (5, 3)' — a centre and a point label fused with no separator, then the same information is repeated in the real sentence. The stray 'G' welded to 'centre (2, 1)' is especially confusing and makes the reader re-parse the whole opening.
fix: Delete the leading 'centre (2, 1)G (5, 3)'; the sentence 'Point G(5, 3) is enlarged by scale factor −1, centre (2, 1). What are the coordinates of G'?' already states the point and the centre.

step: centre (0, 6)(9, 0) A triangle is enlarged by scale factor 1/3, centre (0, 6). Vertex (9, 0) maps to:
why: The stem begins with 'centre (0, 6)(9, 0)' run together before the sentence, duplicating the centre and vertex that appear again in the instruction. A weaker reader treats it as part of the question and stalls on the unlabelled numbers.
fix: Remove the leading 'centre (0, 6)(9, 0)'; the sentence 'A triangle is enlarged by scale factor 1/3, centre (0, 6). Vertex (9, 0) maps to:' is complete on its own.

step: (2, 1)(4, 2)(1, −2)(2, −4) Describe the single transformation that maps (2, 1) to (1, −2) and (4, 2) to (2, −4).
why: Four coordinate pairs are strung together with no spacing or labels at the start of the stem before the instruction begins. This coordinate soup is the hardest of the set to parse and forces a full re-read to locate the actual question.
fix: Delete the leading '(2, 1)(4, 2)(1, −2)(2, −4)'; the sentence 'Describe the single transformation that maps (2, 1) to (1, −2) and (4, 2) to (2, −4).' carries all the coordinates.

step: centre (1, 1)(4, 2) A shape at (4, 2) is enlarged by scale factor −2, centre (1, 1). Where is the image?
why: The stem opens with 'centre (1, 1)(4, 2)' fused together before the sentence, repeating the centre and point given in the readable instruction. The reader must strip the unlabelled prefix to reach the question.
fix: Remove the leading 'centre (1, 1)(4, 2)'; the sentence 'A shape at (4, 2) is enlarged by scale factor −2, centre (1, 1). Where is the image?' stands alone.

step: The + case: 2x − 3 = 2, so 2x = 5 and x = [box=2.5, NO label]  /  The − case: 2x − 3 = −2, 2x = 1, x = [box=0.5, NO label]
why: Both terminal x-boxes are unflagged decimals reached by halving an odd number (5÷2, 1÷2). The line jumps straight from '2x = 5' to 'x =' without showing the ÷2, so a struggling student who expects a whole-number x may write 2 (or '2 remainder 1') rather than 2.5, and 0 rather than 0.5. Nothing in the prose signals the answer is a decimal.
fix: Add label "(a decimal)" to both the x=2.5 and x=0.5 boxes.

why: 10 ÷ 4 gives a decimal, but unlike the other iteration boxes in this pack there is no 'to 2 d.p.' cue on this step. A struggling student may write 2 (or '2 r 2') and then carry the wrong value into the next step's denominator.
fix: Add label "(a decimal)" to the x₁ box.

step: Gradient = rise ÷ run = (-12) ÷ 8 =  [box=-1.5, NO label]
why: This is the only non-integer answer in the whole pack — every other box is a whole number. A struggling student who works out -12 ÷ 8 may be unsure whether to type a decimal (-1.5), a fraction (-12/8) or a mixed number, because nothing signposts that the answer form has switched to a decimal here.
fix: Add label '(a decimal)' to the box.

step: ACBxy0Show that \(A(1, 3)\), \(B(5, 7)\) and \(C(3, 5)\) are collinear. What is the gradient of \(AB\)?
why: The question stem opens with a garbled token 'ACBxy0' (stray diagram/axis labels A, C, B, x, y, 0 fused into the sentence). A struggling student sees broken, nonsense text jammed against the word 'Show' and cannot tell where the actual question begins; it reads as a rendering error.
fix: Delete the 'ACBxy0' prefix so the stem reads: 'Show that A(1, 3), B(5, 7) and C(3, 5) are collinear. What is the gradient of AB?'

step: Show that ... are collinear ... / check collinear: gradient AC = (5 - 3) ÷ (3 - 1) = 2 ÷ 2 =
why: 'Collinear' appears in both the stem and the final check step but is never defined. A struggling 15-year-old is unlikely to know it means the points all lie on one straight line, so the point of the question (and why equal gradients prove it) stays opaque even though the box arithmetic is fully built.
fix: Gloss it on first use, e.g. 'collinear (all lie on one straight line)'.

step: Now the area: ½ × 14 × 15 × sin 53.1° =  [box=84, NO label]
why: This is the final area answer but, unlike every other area problem in the pack (bronze[2], bronze[3], bronze[6], silver[3]) which end with a 'Check the units: area is in cm²' step, gold[3] has no unit here and no prose stating cm². A student cannot tell if 84 is cm or cm², and the number could be mistaken for a length.
fix: cm²

step: Inverse sine: sin⁻¹(0.4302) =  [box=25.5, NO label]
why: This is the answer to the question (angle B). No 'degrees' label and no degree symbol anywhere in the step; the student has just typed a decimal (0.4302), so they cannot tell the calculator output 25.5 is an angle in degrees rather than another decimal.
fix: degrees

step: Inverse cosine: cos⁻¹(0.6) =  [box=53.1, NO label]
why: This is the final answer (angle A). No 'degrees' label and no degree symbol in the step, immediately after typing the decimal 0.6 — a struggling student can't tell 53.1 is in degrees.
fix: degrees

step: Inverse cosine: cos⁻¹(0.8148) =  [box=35.4, NO label]
why: This is the final answer (angle C). No 'degrees' label and no degree symbol in the step, following the decimal 0.8148 — the magnitude/unit of 35.4 is ambiguous to a struggling reader.
fix: degrees

step: Inverse sine: sin⁻¹(0.6667) =  [box=41.8, NO label]
why: This is the final answer (the acute angle P). No 'degrees' label and no degree symbol in the step, right after the decimal 0.6667 — nothing signals that 41.8 is degrees.
fix: degrees

step: Second angle (ambiguous case): 180° − 66.7° =  [box=113.3, NO label]
why: This is one of the two required answers, yet its sibling box (first angle, sin⁻¹ result) IS labelled 'degrees' while this one is not. The inconsistency implies the two answers might be different kinds of number; a final angle answer should carry the unit.
fix: degrees

step: Angle A: cos⁻¹(0.6) =  [box=53.1, NO label]
why: The inverse-cosine output has no degree signal in the box or step (only the operand 0.6, a decimal). The 'Angle A:' prefix tells the student it is an angle but not that 53.1 is in degrees, which they need before feeding it into sin 53.1° next.
fix: degrees

step: Square root: √19 =  [box=4.4, NO label]
why: Final answer to a word problem where both distances are in km ('3 km', '5 km', 'How far apart are they?'). The box has no 'km' and no unit appears in the step, so a student juggling the bearings problem gets no reminder of what 4.4 measures.
fix: km

step: Square root: √67.1661 =  [box=8.2, NO label]
why: Final answer (AC) to a ship-bearings word problem measured in km ('8 km', '6 km'). No 'km' label and no unit in the step, so the distance answer's unit is left to the student to infer.
fix: km

step: Check the third angle: 180° − 35° − 25.5° =  [box=119.5, NO label]
why: This is the LAST value the student computes, but it is NOT the answer (the answer is angle B = 25.5°). Labelling it 'Check the third angle' is misleading — it computes a different angle (angle C) rather than verifying B — so a struggling student may write 119.5 as their final answer.
fix: Relabel to make clear this is a separate angle, not the answer, e.g. 'Angle C (a separate angle, not the one asked for): 180° − 35° − 25.5° =', or drop the 'Check' framing.

step: θ = sin⁻¹(0.7) =  [box=44.4, NO label]
why: This is an angle answer with no 'degrees' label. A struggling student sees a bare 44.4 sitting next to other decimal ratio boxes (0.7) and cannot tell it is an angle rather than a length or another ratio — exactly the ambiguity the review targets.
fix: Add label 'degrees' to the box.

step: θ = tan⁻¹(8 ÷ 6) =  [box=53.1, NO label]
why: Angle answer with no 'degrees' label. The surrounding boxes in this walk are decimals (1.33), so 53.1 has nothing marking it as an angle.
fix: Add label 'degrees' to the box.

step: Add all three: 9 + 16 + 144 =  [box=169, NO label]
why: Finding a cuboid's diagonal uses the 3D result d = √(l²+w²+h²), i.e. squaring and summing THREE dimensions. Unlike gold[0], this problem has no intro; the step 'Add all three' presupposes the space-diagonal rule the walk never builds, so a student who only knows flat Pythagoras won't know why three squares are added.
fix: Add an intro like gold[0]'s: 'A cuboid's diagonal uses all three edges — d = √(l²+w²+h²) — so square all three lengths, add them, then square-root.'

step: θ = sin⁻¹(0.7) =  [box=44.4, NO label]  (and silver[3] tan⁻¹)
why: sin⁻¹ / tan⁻¹ (inverse trig) appears here for the first time with no explanation of what the notation means or which calculator button to press. The lesson built forward-trig (sin30° = 0.5) but never introduced going backwards from a ratio to an angle.
fix: Add a line before the step: 'To find the angle, use inverse sine — the sin⁻¹ (2nd-Function sin) button.' Do the same for tan⁻¹ in silver[3].

step: sin40°, to 2 d.p. =  [box=0.64, NO label]
why: bronze[6]/[7] handed the ratio to the student ('sin30° = 0.5'). This is the first step that expects them to produce sin40° themselves, with no instruction to use a calculator or to be in degrees mode. A struggling student won't know where 0.64 comes from.
fix: Reword to 'Use your calculator (in degrees mode): sin40°, to 2 d.p. ='.

step: sin30° = 0.5, and the opposite is the hypotenuse times this. First write the hypotenuse:  [box=18, NO label]
